utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madame Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Ladies and gentlemen, I am indeed capable of following the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Patricia Sellers for the Prosecution. Today we have co-counsel, Mr. Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and also Ms. Joanne Richardson, our case manager, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. Good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the Defence for Mr. Naser Oric. We have our legal assistant, Miss Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? None.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. None from our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a question. I'm still in a position whereby standing up for a long time is a problem for me, so if you would kindly allow me, I would like to be sitting down during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish those are all the problems that we have to solve, Madam Vidovic. So let's bring in the witness, please. She has already gone, yes. Do you have an idea what time you expect to finish your in-chief? MR. DI FAZIO: The best-laid plans. Yes, I hope to finish, as I had agreed with Madam Vidovic, I did a careful minute by minute calculation last night that brings me to about 11.30, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It must be quite boring, actually. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll -- I worked out an order of priority. I will do everything I can to try and finish it by about that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that more or less because this is a witness who is definitely important for the Prosecution, but probably more important for the Defence. So let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Meholjic and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is interpretation getting to you loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, please make yourself comfortable. Sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your testimony but before we do so, let's go into private session for a minute or so. I need to explain something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Meholjic, yesterday we made good progress and today we need to make even better progress, and I appreciated the way you kept your answers reasonably brief and pertinent and I ask that you assist me again today by doing that. And we will, I think if we do that, we will meet the targets that we've set for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a military action in March of 1993. I don't think it is in dispute that in that time Serb forces attacked the Srebrenica enclave and I understand that there were two Serb corps that you dealt with, you personally. The Valjevo Corps and the Uzice corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you very briefly have a look at Exhibit P518, and using a marker pen that some kind person will supply to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had it here, but ... MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, just before you actually look at the map and mark it, I just want you to tell me if this is correct. The Serb forces had been attacking Srebrenica more intensely in the period of time leading up to March of 1993? In the immediate period before March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In March of 1993, it appeared to you and to others in the Srebrenica enclave, that the Serb forces might overrun the enclave? Is that correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: A meeting was called -- I'm not going to go into the details of the meeting now -- but a meeting was called and you were -- found yourself in the position -- and I will get back to this later -- but you found yourself in the position of meeting the Serb forces that were advancing from the south?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't meet with the Serb forces at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I been cooperating with them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- just refer to the meeting, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let him explain what happened, very briefly. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what was the result or the consequence after that, the events after that meeting. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, all right. Well, let's go to the meeting itself. Madam Usher, if you would just leave the map there, I might not actually need to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't take it as a criticism, Mr. Di Fazio. The thing is I appreciate you were trying to condense it to save time, but -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- but it was counter productive. MR. DI FAZIO: That's -- I -- I thank you Your Honour. I'm grateful to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay, the meeting. The Serb forces are poised to overrun the enclave and was it the case there was consternation and worry amongst the Muslim forces that were supposed to resist them?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now was there a meeting held to discuss this very issue?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, tell us about how many people were there? Was it a small or large meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large meeting. Perhaps some 200 of us. I can't give you the exact figure. I didn't count, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was Mr. Oric present? Was Zulfo Tursunovic present? And other members of the Srebrenica armed forces?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what was the major topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main topic of discussion was the situation after the offensive, not after. But in the course of the Serb offensive and they had reinforcements provided by the armed forces from Serbia, and the situation that we found ourselves in -- if you allow me I would like to elaborate a little bit. The attack started from the direction of Skelani, across Kraglijivoda to Zelani Jadar and we're talking about an area of about 10 kilometres long and fifteen kilometres wide. So this was an offensive which pushed back the fighters that were there and the citizens as well. So basically, I mean Srebrenica was full of people in this valley and they all fled and we found ourselves in a situation which the armed forces did not want to obey -- did not want to put up any resistance, so we discussed that. And Naser listened to what the commanders had to say, what their -- their view of the situation was and -- would you like to ask a question? Or do you want me to provide you with a brief summary? I can continue. At that meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just keep it as brief as possible. And tell us what was concluded in that meeting, the conclusions reached, decisions taken. Very shortly please, precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly. At the meeting, the assessment was that the people who were in charge of the upper area, the area that fell were of the view that it was impossible to defend the area and Naser said, well, okay. We are unable to defend the area. I think he found it very difficult and psychologically speaking it was extremely difficult for him. At that stage I said, "Well this is the end of it." There was snow on the ground. I said the population will be massacred. And Naser at that stage appointed me commander of the defence line Pusmulici, Ljubisavici, Bukova Glava and he subordinated all the other forces from the area up there. To me -- I mean, there was still commanders of their units but I had the main responsibility for that area and I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Now, you say he did this. Did he do this publicly at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you, in due course, take up your command position and go into action and defend the enclave for a period of about 7 days along with the forces that had been put at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it wasn't a command post. There was no command post there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please repeat because we didn't hear the last word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, yes, I took over. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, I understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said, they said it was Pod Bokan [phoen], that's the part that interpreters did not hear. Could the witness elaborate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was no command post. You had to be on the front line and the front line was Bukve. There was nothing else. We were on the front line. We had nothing to fall back on. We had no tents. Nothing. It was -- it was out in the field. It was under the trees, in the forest. Maybe I made myself clear now. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, okay. That's fine. I wasn't talking about an actual physical command post. I was talking about your position as a commander. That's the sort of position I was talking about, but don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On the 7th of April, did the Serb forces with draw following heavy fighting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to turn to another topic, but vaguely related. You've given extensive evidence over the last two days of your attending meetings for planning of military actions, and also you have testified, yesterday, briefly, in passing, on the lack of uniforms and the lack of good clothing that the soldiers, the fighters, the Muslim fighters had. I think the effect of your evidence was that they were poorly dressed. And that's not in controversy in this case. The Muslim forces that did fight, how did they distinguish themselves from one another and from the enemy, in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we distinguished ourselves because we agreed that we would place a piece of cloth, a band, an arm band. For this action it would be yellow. For another one, red. And then green, or what have you. Let me just make this clear. You would have a piece of cloth, a narrow strip of cloth, and we would wear it as arm bands. We had no other distinctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And when would it be decided to wear these particular ribbons or cloths, at the pre-planning sessions? Or at some other stage?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we agreed we would go and then we would agree on the markings, because we did not all know one another, so it was a distinctive did sign of recognition. So when we made the agreement, okay, we'll go tomorrow and then we all made our own home bands at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And just on this topic, last question, did the colours vary from action to action or were they always the same?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. I would now like you to turn your attention, please, to communications. Do you know of a place called the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where -- I suppose in Srebrenica you mean? MR. DI FAZIO: In Srebrenica. Sorry, of course I meant Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know what you were taking it for granted but for the transcript and for the record it needs to be stated. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In 1992, were there any radio equipment facilities in that building?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some equipment which had been repaired and it was there. Not straight away, not in the beginning but at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever use the radio, just answer me yes or no, did you ever actually use it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was that to contact your family?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know who operated the radio in the PTT building? Who -- what operators they were? And their names, if you know them.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the names. One was called Naser. I don't know his family name. And I know he works in Tuzla at the PTT at Tuzla, that's his job now. And the other is Mevlo Suljagic, a cousin there. He's from Bratunac as well, the municipality of Bratunac. But he was a professional postal worker before the war, so he was familiar with the stuff, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were they soldiers or fighters in the Srebrenica TO?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they were civilians. They never went anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was access to that -- the radio facilities, whenever it operated, free, in the sense that anyone could go and use it? Or did one have to obtain some sort of permission?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't free for everyone. Had everyone been using it as they pleased, well, it was only natural for the staff and the municipality and the Presidency set it up for the communication needs and, of course, if there was an exceptional situation with the special approval people could do that. And then at a later stage we had a second radio station where citizens could also go and use it. It was at the centre of town, near the town hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But forgetting about the second one that you've mentioned, sticking with the one in the PTT building you said access wasn't automatic. You controlled access to the radio station, to the one in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the command and Naser.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And this second radio station that you mentioned, the one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please, because it seems that in this context he has already mentioned another Naser and now he says the commander, Naser. Perhaps we need to be specific. Which Naser are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oric. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I think he also said the command and Naser. It's come out as the commander Naser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's the command and Naser. That's what I have in the transcript. If that is not correct please draw my attention straight away because this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it was just in your question it came out that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes, yes. All right. Thank you, Mr. Jones. The system I would like to be in place when it comes to mistakes in the transcripts. Small, minor mistakes that can be rectified after, please don't stand up and mention them as we go along. Those can be remedied without any problems. Mistakes which are of essence and need a feedback from the witness in particular, then, yes, please do stand up straight away and point them out to us without -- with the least delay possible. All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, sorry for the interruption. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The second radio station, was that a much freer radio station and did the citizens have much less restricted or greater access to it? Was it for --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it mainly for the people of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. Thanks. Did you, in 1992 or 1993, ever see a Paket, Paket radio system being used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We want to understand first and foremost what Paket is. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Let me put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see any --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Motorola or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely why I wanted you to explain first what you mean by a Paket system. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see any radio system or become aware of any radio system that had encryption or code -- or encryption devices built into it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was something that we called a Paket device, it had a screen like a computer. There was a girl, and this is what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that's the thing that I want to know about. When did you become aware of that device operating? Was it in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. There it was, but not from the beginning. Naser would know better than me. I don't want to lie to you. I don't know whether it was towards the end of combat activities, before Srebrenica became an enclave or after that. I really don't know. I know that later on we had it, because I used it to send some messages, or reports to -- something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Well I don't want to push the matter any further than I can. Can you answer this question: Could you say that it was in use and in existence in Srebrenica before March of 1993, or are you in a position not to be able to say that with any reliability?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any degree of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Well, who controlled access to that system, whenever it was in place?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system belonged to the TO staff. And the person who was working with it was Nadjet Hamidovic [phoen]. He was the first one. He came from Tuzla. I suppose he may have brought it with him, but I can't be sure of that. I don't know how this was brought and when. In any case, this man was not in Srebrenica before. How he came and when, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Before I move on to a whole new topic can I briefly take you back to the ribbons that you mentioned. I think you gestured during your evidence that they wore ribbons, the soldiers wore ribbons on their arms. Is that correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. It was not prescribed whether this band should be worn on the left or on the right hand. People wore it in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Did they ever wear it around their foreheads? Wear them around their foreheads?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such things. There were people who did it on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: But those people were a few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit P84, please. And it's available in Sanction, if Your Honours please. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just so that we're all clear. You will have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: This is a handwritten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have both, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have both, Mr. Di Fazio, at least I'm speaking for myself. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think usually we get -- I have got the English and the original. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. The B/C/S is a handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on each page it has the usual ERN number. Now as you go through the English you will see at various points throughout the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. We know how it works. We have used this document several times already. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, okay. Now, if that can be placed with the witness, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Meholjic, prior to coming to The Hague, had you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to take you to -- sorry, before I go any further. Do you recognise the handwriting or is that unfamiliar to you? You can't say who it is?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise this handwriting. I'm not familiar with it. I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you know -- you remember from proofing, Mr. Meholjic, that there is a computer number on each page of that document. Sometimes it's in one spot. Sometimes it's in another. And it's a long number. Just to make things easy, what you have to look for is the last four numbers and then you will be able to flip through until you find the relevant entry. The first entry that I want to take you to is at 5045. 5045. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, that's page 4 to 6 on -- in the English, page 4 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean four to six. MR. DI FAZIO: Pages four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 4 only? If or referring to 5045, it's only -- it schemes to me to be at least only on page 4 of the English version. MR. DI FAZIO: This topic will cover pages 4 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's different. MR. DI FAZIO: That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Meholjic -- sorry, if you go back to page 5045, at the top you will see that whoever wrote this document is talking about places such as Bjelovac and Fakovici. Then if you go to page 5046, you will see that it is minutes of the 3rd of October. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that. There's something wrong with this. I only have two sentences, which don't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can you look at the top of the page and tell us what is the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I can be of assistance. The Prosecutor has made a mistake in reading the number. Look at the number. You have provided the witness with the wrong page number. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Well let's start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Indeed, in 5045, if you look at the original, there are four lines, two of which, at least on the photocopy, are illegible. I mean, I can't understand what is written in any case. So when he says that, on page -- yes, but what is probably happening is the following, because 5045, the ERN number is in the middle of the page. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't want to dwell too long on this, if Your Honours please. I think I can speed it up by simply asking the witness to skip then 5045 and go to 5046.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Usher, please check that he has 5046. And that has, at the top, "minutes," that's October 1992. And a stamp at the top right corner. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you with us, Mr. Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's a lot easier for us because we have a typed version and you've got that handwritten copy, but if you cast your eyes down through the text, whoever wrote this appears to be talking about the -- something involving Fakovici. Do you see that? If you cast your eye down page 5056. All right? Then if you turn over the page -- okay? Now, do you have page 5047, with the computer number 5047?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, the part that I just want to show you first is at the top of 5047. Now, it starts off with boat crossings will be covered by anti-aircraft machine-gun. Do you see that? That's right at the top of the page, at the very top. Do you see that? Right, have you got it? You're nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Then it goes on: "At the end of the operation destroy the ferry. It would not be good for withdrawal if they stayed in their houses. There must be a medical technician in this group. A doctor in Jagodina. Nadret is to work out a schedule." Now, do you know if Dr. Mujkanovic played any part in events that occurred in Fakovici? I'm not trying to suggest that to you. I just want you to tell us if from independently, from your own knowledge, can you tell us if Dr. Mujkanovic played any role at all in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did play a role. He was in the medical centre down there. He was waiting for the wounded, to assist them. I don't know of any other role that he may have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you go down, further down page 5047, and you will come to point number 9. You see "communications"? Do you see that it's actually should have a number written there. Number 9.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: "Communications." It says "the military police must take mobile radio transmitter and walkie-talkies. They have to be distributed." It says "the command post is at the anti-aircraft machine-gun site and the password was going to be Bosna Djihad." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us if that was the password for Fakovici, Bosna Djihad?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the general picture. I remember generally what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. That's okay. Now, finally, on this section of this document, look at the -- there is an entry for number of troops. Do you see "armour, 45." "Zulfo, 60." "Sefik, 30." Someone else, 50. And then there is the name "Hakija, 60." Now, I'm sure I'll be corrected if I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- but you have testified, haven't you, that -- you've already testified that sixty people -- sixty men were what you provided for the Fakovici action. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to provide a clarification. They asked me how many men I could provide. I said I could provide 60. Nobody ordered me to provide 60. I don't know how many troops other people pledged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's fine. But in the pre-planning part of this, of matters before the attack on Fakovici, you were offering, providing 60 men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are at this, Mr. Di Fazio, let's clarify this. The 4th one, the one below Sefik, can you read that name? Whether it is 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Senahid, S-e-n-a-h-i-d, Senahid, 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the last one, after the one below Sakib?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P-O-T. I suppose it stands for Potocari. It can't be anything else as far as I know. There is no name that would start with these three letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I now want you to go just a little bit further through the document. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, the part that I am looking at now, you will find at pages 7 through to 9 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The part that I want to show you, Mr. Meholjic, is -- starts with computer number 5050. 5050. And it is apparently, on the face of this document, the minutes of a meeting of the War Presidency on the 14th of October, 1992. Do you see that, at the top of 5050?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And then underneath that is an agenda. It says: "Organisation and functioning of the military and civilian authorities."

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you see the next sentence, "the meeting was called to order by Osman Osmanovic. He said that we're faced with the problem problems in the functioning of the system, the War Presidency, two staffs, civilian protection." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you weren't at this meeting, were you? You weren't present?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Discussion related to that topic continues through 5050 and then turn the page to 5051. And there is, apparently on the face of this document, further discussion related to that topic. Midway through 5051 there is an entry that relates to Naser, apparently, and "so far all the problems have been due to a lack of organisation," "boils down to the need for everybody to do his bit." "You can argue about power later." "Come to your senses." "Let's organise. Dig in." And so on. Then Osman says: Let's be more concrete. Let's put names in each structure. Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to read this. I can see the paper. Well, you have read out some bits but it's very difficult for me to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I know, it's easier for us, hard for you. You've got the handwritten version. But just bear with me. I will try and get you through it as fast as I can. Just look at those details. You've already touched upon this topic, but just very briefly go through it again. Hajrudin Avdic, was he indeed president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you put that question to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what they called him. That's how he was here referred to, president of the War Presidency. I don't know whether he did the job, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is one point which, I think if it is not clarified, it may lead to confusion. My learned friend started by saying this was minutes apparently of the War Presidency meeting. It is clearly -- it is a joint meeting, War Presidency and staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I'm right. I think that does need to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. The second thing is that question was put to you yesterday and he gave you more or less the same answer. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So where we can economise, let's economise. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Let's move on from this topic. Let's go to 5052.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you see that? Page 5052?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. 5052 about midway down the page there is an entry relating to, apparently, notes of some sort of conversation. And you seem to be the topic. Naser: What we should do with Hakija's unit? They refused to give snipers to Zulfo and to go to Fakovici. Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now look up from the document and have a think about events from Fakovici. Did you or did you not -- and answer this question from your own memory, not what the document says, but from your own memory, your own knowledge -- did you, or did you refuse to provide snipers or rifles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have him first confirm that the Hakija that is mentioned there is himself and not someone else. MR. DI FAZIO: Well ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am the Hakija in question. There was no one else by that name. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, forget what the document says and tell us, from what your mind tells you, your own memory tells you, did you provide -- did you not provide snipers or rifles for the Fakovici action? Don't let the document sway you. Just tell us what your memory tells you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember us giving snipers. We did provide some weapons. There was not enough weapons to go around, so I believe that we gave some to Zulfo's men, I think. My deputy, Velid, was at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's move on. Sorry. Sorry. Just while we're there. Just keep going down the page. You see that there is an entry next to the name of Naser, the operations staff should secure coverage of Zalazje, Salatusa [phoen]. Were those towns close to or involved in any way, as far as you're aware, of the -- in the military action on Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you please repeat the names of the places. Either I have not heard you well, or you have mispronounced the names. In any case I can't locate those names in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to press that matter. Let's move to somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There is no need for that. If you said Zaluzje, this is not a town or anything. It's just a village in the area of Bratunac municipality, in an entirely opposite direction from Fakovici. And I really don't see the point of mentioning this place. The distance between the two may be as many as 20 kilometres. That's why I've asked you to repeat the question. I'm not afraid of any of your questions. I will answer anything, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Di Fazio. Look at six lines from the bottom, please, of the page. That's where you find the names of the two places. Six lines, exactly six lines from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see that. From the bottom of the page, if you're talking about page 5052?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. Six lines before the end, can you bring the page here, Madam Usher, and I will show you the words. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zaluzje, yes. But I don't know what the word before means. The person who has translated the document for you must have taken a long time to analyse the word. I believe that it says the coverage of Zaluzje. What it means, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And one further thing, by way of clarification more than anything else. The next line starts with "Hakija." And then Hakija is supposed to say "Mirza's team," et cetera. I got the impression that in the course of this meeting you were not present and that you were represented by Velid. How come we see your name there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe my name was mentioned. Whenever somebody said Hakija, that meant my men, irrespective of who was there. If somebody mentioned Zulfo, that referred to Zulfo's men. Somebody mentioning Naser, referred to Naser's men. Not these people personally, as individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I raise the issue because in the English text there is a colon after "Hakija" which you don't find in the original. In the original there is a comma behind "Hakija," so I just wanted to make this clear, that the English text should not be read as to necessarily mean that he was present and that the next words are attributed to him. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise it is not important, but I just wanted to make sure of that. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, the next part I want to take you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance? I have not read the entire thing. This probably doesn't have anything to do with the action up there. Maybe this refers to the coverage -- and I remember one part -- patrol was supposed to be sent there, to these Muslim villages which are very close to Bratunac. There was nobody in charge of these villages. There were no Serbs or Muslims there. So we were supposed to organise patrols that would last for seven days and after that the Bratunac unit would be set up and we would all allocate men for that unit that would be sent down there to guard that area, the area there where they hale from. If I have interpreted the whole thing well. This is a preliminary action for something that would ensue, that would follow. This meant that patrols would be sent down there and cover the area while people spontaneously go there to harvest wheat or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to go to the page -- the part of the document with computer number 5056? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, you will see this at Page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, this is, apparently, the minutes of a meeting of the Srebrenica Armed Forces Operation Staff held 15 October, 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Mr. Osman starts off by saying: "We have to secure the liberated" - liberated - "territory." And he talks about the priority keeping the line towards Bratunac and the most critical situation is in Zaluzje and Likari. And the area should be held by units from Srebrenica and Solocusa. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Solocusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. That's okay I'm just taking you through it until we get to the part of it. The next sentence the Zalazje area will be guarded by the following units. Srebrenica, Hakija. A part of Akif's unit and Solocusa. Now, can you shed any light on that entry? Did you ever contribute to, men to the guarding of something in Zalazje around October 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. If you move down into the next paragraph it starts "since winter is approaching" do you see that? Right. Now it continues, "A house in Zalazje is going to be arranged to house personnel. The unit from Solocusa are going to have their meals at home. Hakija's and Akit's" -- maybe Akif, I don't know, "but Hakija's units will move to Zabarija [phoen]. Hakija will do the first shift. Solocusa, the second." Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Does that spark any memory? Can you shed any light on that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what I had told you before. This is a free area, so to say. Which was ethnically clear. And Akif's unit is being mentioned. They continued to call it Atif even though he was no longer there. He had been killed. But the unit is still being referred to as his unit. We went down there to secure the front line or patrol the area around Voljevica and Zaluzje because there were calls from citizens to the effect that they wanted to go back to their homes. And after perhaps one shift we gave as many people as we had from this area, from our respective units. They stayed there for a while and then they were attacked by Chetniks and they fell. And then they left and nothing happened. I don't know if I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You have, that's fine. Thank you very much for that explanation. Continue now in the document to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just before we leave this page. Could you please ask the witness with regard to number five. It speaks of "it is forbidden for soldiers to move from one area to another." But the word in Serbo-Croat is, does is say soldiers or fighters? And whether these people who are addressed here had this band or apron or something around? MR. DI FAZIO: Does Your Honour mean the people located in these guard duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: When these speak of soldiers here, what is the English? Is there an original word for it and whether these people had some sort of marking. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've been directed to the areas of interest by His Honour. Now, first of all, look at entry number five. It is -- just read it out for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is forbidden for soldiers to move from one unit, presumably" -- I can't see it because the photocopy is of poor quality. Without the approval of the commanders. Well, it happened at a certain period of time. The term soldier, and the person taking notes and being in charge of the minutes, I did say in the beginning that we were no professional soldiers, but we were using these terms. So actually fighter would be more appropriate. A soldier is in the barracks. There is structure of command and orders, et cetera. But these people are fighters. So the way I see it, this is not the appropriate term. It is not soldiers we are talking about, but fighters. And at that stage some people started to choose what units they wanted to go to and that's probably the reason why this entry is here. I mean, in order to indicate to people that they couldn't move from one unit to another without clearing it with the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other question: Would these fighters, called soldiers in the text, wore the bands, the coloured bands or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Those arm bands were only worn in the course of action. Not all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not wear them every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The next area that I want to take you to you will find bears computer number 5060. If Your Honours please, 14 and mainly page 15 in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, if you go to 5060, 5060, you will see that this part of the document apparently deals with a meeting on the 30th of October, 1992. 5060.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. That's just to establish the background. I don't need to trouble you any more with 5060. Turn the page over to 5061. 5061. Do you have that? Look at the top --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- the very top of the page. The writing here may not be very clear.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't clear, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I won't bother about that. Do you see Roman numeral II at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Go a little bit further down, you get to Roman numeral III, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, it ostensibly appears to be some sort of record of conversation. The people speaking, Osman someone called Nijaz, someone called Ramiz, Zulfo, Hamid, and then Zulfo. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Zulfo starts: "There are few armed men in Srebrenica. Hakija is stubborn and works in cooperation with Zepa and" - possibly the word Konjevic Polje - "bypassing our command. He promised all sorts of things and did something completely different. Why did he distribute pigs and sugar to Serbian families. There is a guy in Puzmolici [phoen] or Meho." Now, do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm interested in the pigs. What happened with respect to pigs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my men were out in the field and there were some stray pigs. And they chased those pigs and they said, what do we do with them? And I said, you should kill them and slaughter them, I mean, and we have Serb families living in towns and we could give them to the Serb families living in Srebrenica. Because they were my fellow citizens and -- well, now that I've already mentioned this, Naser and I agreed, and I must say this, we did agree and afterwards, since many people from outside had come to Srebrenica, we wanted to protect those Serbs. We had guards, we went to visit them and we sat with them and we talked to them and they were pleased to meet Naser as well, because they had not known him from before -- I mean, they knew me because I was born in that town. So we tried to protect them as much as we could. And this is the truth I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people minded the fact that I gave that away. Okay, Zulfo minded. I didn't know it was Zulfo's contribution to the discussion, but I did hear that there was a discussion about what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. I'm interested in this issue of the pigs for various reasons, but this little issue about what you had done with the pigs by giving them to Serbian families, was that a matter of notoriety, well known in Srebrenica? Or was it just a -- some episode?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was widely known. Yes, that was the talk of the town. I was feeding the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about sugar. Did you distribute the sugar to the Serbian families or ...

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There wasn't a whole lot of sugar. We had a little bit and we gave it to them to put a bit of it into the water and get some strength. I mean we were all starving. And the ones who were with us were suffering most because it was very difficult for them to get food. I mean, they could not go and look for food because there were irresponsible individuals around and so we had to help them a little bit. It wasn't too much sugar. I mean a kilo or two. There were not too many of them. Nine families, that was next to nothing. If you mean to say that sugar was coming in from somewhere, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps the witness could tell us, Mr. Di Fazio, where these pigs and the sugar were obtained from. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The question is self-evident. Where did you get them?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had some sugar. I think everybody had a sack full or two of sugar. That's what we kept for our own use. I had it in my own unit because my army was at the barracks. We did not have uniforms, but we did have order. And they had something to eat. I mean, everybody knows that. And I gave it away out of my own kitchen. And as to pigs, I mean it wasn't on the same day. Perhaps you are confused by the fact that apparently there were actions or combat activity somewhere, no. They were in the area of Jadran [phoen]. I believe that if we go back to this date now, I think that this was before Podravanje. So Podravanje is next to Jadro [phoen]. It's another location close to Jader [phoen]. It is an industrial area, Jader, that we held and those pigs crossed over. And they took the pigs and then they, you know, gathered them and then they said, "What do we do?" And I said, "Well, slaughter them and we can give them to the Serbs. We have enough Serbs [sic]." We don't eat pork, but we gave it away to them, so that they could survive. That's what it was about, if you're interested to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you would have more food for yourself left. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Next question, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Go to entry number 5098 and if Your Honours please, you will find this part of the evidence at pages 41 to 42 of the English. 5098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you help the witness, please, 5098. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. At the top of the page you can see that it relates apparently to a meeting held on the 22nd of December, 1992. And it's the analysis of an operation -- is part of the agenda. Under number 1, it says "Naser opened the meeting." Hamo, Zujko [phoen], Soson, and Hakija. "Hakija is especially commended for the performance of his tasks. We liberated the mine but it would have been better if we had not. It has been dispersed. We will especially command Mido [phoen] through the Main Staff." Thinking back, do you know what apparent -- what military operation this might be dealing with?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bjelovac operation, because it was at the same time. So I said Bjelovac, et cetera, to Asasija [phoen]. We had no combat activity because the Serbs had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There is an entry there, apparently belonging to Mr. Naser, Mr. Oric. Well, someone called Naser. I'm sorry. It says that the mine was liberated. Can you -- thinking back, and without reference to this document, can you tell us what happened in relation to the mine at Sase.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. The mine, well two or three -- one or two days later I got there with some of my men. Since one and the aircraft gun was found there, as well as a VBR, as we call it, and you probably use different terminology. Something that is normally placed on the wings of aircraft and the Serbs had taken it and then used it as a VBR. And I had two people working at the mine and they were a bit familiar with this and we were looking for this stuff in order to repair it. And we were looking for the missing pieces of these multiple rocket launchers, and I don't know what happened. I don't know what was supposed to have happened. Nothing. And I believe that a conclusion is, if I may comment on this, if there's no other explanation for the fact that he said it would have been better if we had not. I mean, there was so much hunger, misery, and thirst, and I ran into a man who was carrying a kind of bed and it was very far away from Srebrenica, 15 kilometres, and there was snow, and I asked him, "What are you carrying there?" And he says: "It might be expensive." It's a big thing, but instead of getting a piece of bread, he took a bed. And I don't know what his association was, perhaps some irresponsible people or some leadership or the Presidency who were supposed to take over at a later stage. I really don't know. MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I have to bring you to order. You're not really answering the question that was put to you and you're telling us stories which are very important but not an answer to the question that was put to you. Could you repeat the question and please try to get the witness to it, Mr. Di Fazio. I don't like stopping the witness myself. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What you said was actually interesting, but unfortunately time constraints force us to keep you on a tight -- liberation of the mine. What could that possibly mean?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the situation of the mine before and after. When someone says "we have liberated the mine," in the circumstances that you lived at the time, what did you understand? Or what would you understand "we have liberated the mine"? Did you actually liberate the mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We didn't actually, because they fled themselves. They left themselves, because it is close to Bjelovac and this is what I keep trying to say. It was when the framework of the same action, there was no combat activity. They had gone because I see no dead bodies or anything. There was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, continuing this. Turn over to 5099? MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, you will find that on page 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 42, yes. You have seven more minutes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm hoping to finish this in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I will take you straight down, halfway through 5099 or halfway, or perhaps halfway to two-thirds of the way. There is an entry there "Hakija to keep the full barreled PAT for PVO. " Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that I got this four-barreled weapon because we were being shelled all the time. And I placed it outside the city of Srebrenica in the town of Bojna, and that's where we were shooting at the Chetnik planes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. And the weapon that you took and positioned just outside Srebrenica, did it have four barrels?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a four-barreled anti aircraft gun, 20 millimeters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And the acronym PAT, what does that mean. Can you shed any light on that or not? If you don't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: PAT, it's anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay, fine. What about PVO, can you tell us what that --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anti aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just go a little further down past that entry it is talking about 24 December, Voljevica and Vijoca [phoen] to take something, then it says next entry down, all vehicles taken in Sase will be confiscated. Zulfo is proposing that the vehicles should not be confiscated from soldiers. Soson is requesting one vehicle for his unit. Are you aware of any vehicles being taken during or after the attack in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. All I know is that I brought machine which is used in the construction industry for the loading of ore and sand, and it was parked in front of Domavija. But there was no other use for it. So that vehicle stayed there, parked in front of the hotel. Even after the fall of Srebrenica it stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more entry now and I think that will complete that before the break and we will complete this document. Go to page 5117, if Your Honours please, pages 55 to 56 of the English. It is about quite a way through the document. 5117. All right. Take it from me that the document is apparently referring to something -- a meeting held on the 18th of April 1993. It says that Becir opened and chaired the meeting and you, it would seem that you, from reading this document, that you were present and you gave some sort of speech where you spoke about determining and fortifying front lines. Okay. Do you see that that should be towards the top of 5117?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Go to the bottom of --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- The bottom of that page and you so there is an entry, "Hakija M." Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now I don't want to get into the substance of what happened in March or April. I just wanted to know whether this entry makes sense to you, bearing in mind your memory of those events in March of 1993. Apparently there's some speech or comment attributed to you and it says this: Let us leave the analysis of the operation for some time. Let's do concrete work. The Podravanje line goes as follows: Ljeskovik, Kutuzero Lipovac." Now, is that entry correct? Did indeed the Podravanje line go Ljeskovik, Kutuzero, Lipovac.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I said since we did not hold Podravanje, either us or them, and that was a link to Zepa, I said that we should try, since this was a meeting when combat activities stopped and when UNPROFOR arrived and Srebrenica was declared as a protected enclave, a protected area. And I suggested we gave up those lines and I don't remember Naser being there, but there is a little bit -- something illogical about this, because I think Naser had been wounded the day before. And as to Becir chairing the meeting, first of all, I wouldn't have allowed him to do so, what does he have to tell me? And then there was also something that was not really like that, it is not really clear. We had Ramiz Becirevic at the time who would inform us of what was going on down there and in what way. We were supposed to relinquish the weapons, et cetera. We did not want to lose any territory. We wanted to have a slightly bigger territory. And UNPROFOR is coming and if we were to withdraw from Podravanje and Ljeskovik we would have lost some area in the direction of Zepa and we would be cut off. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay, thanks for that. If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we will have a 30 minute break today for the time being and we will resume soon after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed. Sorry for the delay, but that was due to circumstances beyond our control, very diplomatically put. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm finished now with military actions and there are a few miscellaneous topics I want to deal with. Firstly, can you tell the Trial Chamber if in 1992, 1993 you aware of the presence of any black Mercedes in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who owned or used the black Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used by Naser and the owner was Hamina Ibrahim, whose last name, I don't know. He was from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was only for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what period of time?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether it was a petrol car or a diesel car. If it was a petrol car then it must have been for a short period of time because there was no fuel to be had. That was at the very beginning for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you know a gentleman named Kemo. Nicknamed Kemo, I should say.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemo is his name. I know him. He's from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How far is Pale from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe three kilometres, but this is still the Potocari local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he a -- during the war, 1992 and 1993, was he a fighter, a Muslim fighter? Soldier? Whatever.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know which unit or formation or grouping or organisation of soldiers or fighters he was in?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If he belonged to anybody, he belonged to the Potocari unit. And who his commander was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the Potocari unit, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It changed. The battalion commander down there was -- and I don't know when he was appointed and when this changed. I don't know how the positions overlapped. I did not have the possibility to learn about any of the appointments because nobody was duty-bound to inform me about that. At the end of the war it was Mandja Mrki, whose real first name was Ibrahim, if I am not mistaken. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Prior to the war had this fellow Kemo been a trouble maker in the area, been in trouble with the police and being arrested and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrested him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have any troubles in your dealing with him when you arrested him?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any problems. He did cause problems, but when I appeared all the problems stopped. He was not as brave as one may have believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you -- sorry would Your Honours just bear with me. In 1992 was this man Kemo involved in some episode involving a severed head?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would prefer if my learned friend hadn't led in such a blatant way on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact anything concerning Kemo, I would be grateful if my learned friend would lead as little as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think now that you have said it, Mr. Di Fazio will regulate himself accordingly. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was listening to the Defence counsel's objection and I don't know whether the question was -- were you referring to something that Kemo may have done in 1992? Did I understand your question well? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Did you -- what did you understand that episode to be?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were talking about Kemo carrying a severed head, a head belonging to a Serbian and people were outraged. I didn't see it myself. I only heard about that. It was just rumours. And I don't even know whether that was preceded by any action. I don't know what he did. Whatever he did, only he knows what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sure. I understand that. You didn't see anything to do with this episode, that's clear, right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is not the actual episode itself, but whether it was a matter that was known in the town of Srebrenica. You knew of it. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think this witness should be asked what other people knew. It's not a matter within his knowledge, unless other people told him about it. But to be invited to give an opinion about the general state of knowledge of in the town ask far too vague and speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure, Mr. Di Fazio knows that too and I am sure that the question will be in a way that is permissible and can be answered, otherwise it will not be allowed. MR. DI FAZIO: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you find out about the episode? Who told you, since you didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were talking. My men were talking about it, and they told me about these rumours, according to which Kemo was carrying a severed head. I don't know whether I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You have. Thank you. I will move to another topic. You've given extensive evidence about military actions. In the course of these actions, were Serbian prisoners of war ever seized by Muslim forces, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when I was on the ground and when I returned to the Domavija hotel late in the evening, my men informed me that -- if you can just bear with me a moment. From the area of a village close to Ratkovici, it's a Muslim village whose name escapes me at the moment, that these people from this area brought two or three individuals and they didn't want to hand them over. Down there -- when I say "down there," let me make myself clear. I'm referring to Mrki Mandja, because he was the one involved in some exchanges of dead bodies or living people. And this happened on several occasions. I don't know whether it happened on two or three occasions. I don't want to speculate. Instead of handing them over, they brought them to the hotel and they put them in a room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- that's -- you've got to the point that the issue that I'm interested in. And I just want to organise it a bit. First of all, about when did this episode happen? Was it in 1992? Or 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, before the attack on Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you say "people from this area brought two or three individuals". Now, what people brought them? Who brought them and where did they bring them?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the village is Poznanovici and people from this village, who had their Territorial Defence there or something to that effect, they brought them over and they gave them to Amir Mehmedovic. Those were Amir's relatives who brought these people, and Amir was rather close to me in respect of the Command Staff, he was one of my men or close to my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And where did they bring these Serb POWs? Where, actually where? To the Domavija? To somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Domavija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you said that they brought them -- sorry, yes, you did say already they brought them to the hotel. They put in a room. Now, continue your story. What happened after that, they're all brought in.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, my men informed me about that. One of my men, who later on died or was killed, his name was Salko Hublic, also known as Hegel [as interpreted], he ran up to me and he told me: There is Behadil there. He intends to beat these people up there. Behadil was one of my men. He was a member of my unit. I ran up to the room and I beat Behadil in front of everybody and I asked them whether anybody else had touched them before. They said "No." Then I said, "Don't lie to me. I need to hear the truth." I don't know their names, but one of them was a super in the village [as interpreted], in Ratkovici. On the following day, I issued an order for these people to be taken over to Mrki Mandja and to be handed over to them. And this is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I want to know is this, if you can assist us. Why did these men, who had these Serb POWs in their custody, bring them to your men at the Domavija hotel? Why did that happen? Why were they taken to your men?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were neighbours. These people brought their neighbours over. And they said: We are sorry for them, if we hand them over, they will be beaten. They just assumed -- they said Mirza would beat them. And they didn't want this to happen. And then I had this problem with Behadil on top of everything. And the only thing I could do with Behadil is to send him away. There were no institutions. I could not report him to anybody, to punish him for what he had done. I just beat him up and that was it. If these people are still alive, I'm sure that they can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, you just said your people brought them over because they were former neighbours and you felt sorry for them and you said: "And they thought that if we hand them over, they will be beaten." Hand them over to who? Whom?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this guy, Mirza.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did Mirza have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was the commander of the military police and Mrki Mandja, as far as we knew, was involved in some sort of exchanges. He was entrusted with that task by the staff or somebody. Somebody gave him that task. And it was a well-known fact. Everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So Mrki was a member of the -- is it your position that Mrki was a member of the armed forces of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was, to the same extent as all of us were. He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And he was the fellow in charge of exchanges? Is that your position? Or have I understood you correctly? Or not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his name always came up when people were talking about exchanges. I suppose he was in charge. I never attended a meeting at which somebody said that he would be in charge of that. However, according to my information, it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've testified earlier that you were made police chief in, I think, April of 1993, police chief for the whole of Srebrenica. Is that correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thereafter did you become a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by virtue of my function or position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you attend meetings of the War Presidency from April 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how often were meetings held?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the situation. Sometimes all of us would meet. Sometimes the chief would call a number of people that he needed for a certain thing. And there was a meeting every fortnight maybe or once a month. Generally speaking it -- these meetings would take place two times a month, but I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Did Mr. Oric attend meetings when you were present?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes he was there and sometimes Ramiz was there in his place, to substitute for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that Ramiz Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was -- apart from attending meetings, can you tell the Trial Chamber if Mr. Oric was or was not a member of that War Presidency that you've just been speaking of from that point, April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. We set up this Presidency pursuant to a decree. Not pursuant to any elections. This decree was published in the official gazette. The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had issued a decision on who the members of the War Presidency would be. Namely, the commander, the chief of the police station, the head of the municipal Assembly, the secretary of the secretariat for national defence, also presidents of various political parties. From the SDA there was the president. There was also the president of the SDP. So this body differed from the body that existed before. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P296, please. It's on the Sanction thing. Just before it is handed to the witness, can I have a look at the original of the B/C/S, please, the B/C/S version? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
