utterances.text: Yes. We would like to see it as well. You can put it on the ELMO. Let ... Yes. Precisely. I'm asking to see it because in the English translation of it, at the bottom, there is "Chief," and then "Hakija Meholjic." In the B/C/S version the last line there shows "JS, Nacelik," [as interpreted] and nothing else. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I wanted to verify that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. If Your Honours please, sometimes documents are, in this institution, are later typed up and those versions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My suspicion is that this is photocopying, attributable to photocopying. That's what I think, because it's -- the first line on the top is two further down compared with other pages. So I think probably the last line has disappeared from -- but perhaps you can dig up the original in your records. MR. DI FAZIO: I will certainly look into the matter, and if there is a better B/C/S version we will produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Meholjic, please have a look at that document. Just acquaint yourself with it. The first question is, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do you know who created this document?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now there is just one or two points in the document that I want to take you to. The document speaks for itself. It is dated June 1995. And it is a -- appears to be a short report on the situation in Srebrenica. And in the second paragraph of the document, you take -- you refer to some history, saying that UNPROFOR entered Srebrenica in April 1993. Civilian authorities organised. And then you say: "A misdemeanour court, office of the public Prosecutor, lower court and municipal prison were established." Now you're saying in this document, as I read it anyway, happened after April 1993. Can you tell us, if I'm indeed correct, how long after April 1993 those institutions were set up?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the justice ministry should have all of that, because we sent a request to the justice ministry in order for the judges to be appointed, because the judges had fled. We had no judges. And for the setting up of the prison unit, because previously the person for the municipality of Srebrenica was in Tuzla. But we found ourselves in a situation in which we were unable to send people to Tuzla and the justice ministry appointed judges and the commander of that, let's say, prison police, and they were separate. I didn't allow for them to be within the structure of a regular police force, as a member of the Presidency. Apart from that, we had no other contacts with them. And it was perhaps -- well, two months later, two, two-and-a-half months it took. But I think you might be able to find the document pointing out the exact date somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, if I just might address you briefly on the issue of the B/C/S version. Our case manager has very helpfully solved the problem. There is an extra page ending in ERN number 2166, copies are being made of that now and we will have them for you before the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. And I thank the case manager too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, did these miss demeanour courts office of public Prosecutors lower courts and municipal prison actually function and establish -- actually function following the establishment? In other words, did they operate, deal with cases, deal with prosecutions, deal with imprisonments?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From time to time did that involve members of the army, the Bosnian army who were involved in criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that for what you might call the more common criminal offences, the usual range of criminal offences recognisable in most countries, assaults, robberies, drunkenness, fighting, that sort of thing? Theft?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Go to the end of the paragraph, again the second paragraph, and there is a sentence there that says this: "Whenever members of the BH army were involved the court would immediately inform the military court in Tuzla, which would then accept and extend the detention. The detainees were kept in the municipal prison in Srebrenica. The court did not hold trials, so there were no convicted persons." Now, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what you meant when you wrote that. Which court would inform the military court in Tuzla, how did it do that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a mistranslation here because it says in this text: Whenever it was about the members of the armed forces of the BH, the judges were to inform. Not myself. But the judges were supposed to relay that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right, fine. Fine. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever the minister of the interior papers were signed, it was not up to me any more, but the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, do you have any knowledge, actual personal knowledge of soldiers being involved in some criminal offence and the judges informing the military court in Tuzla? Can you tell us if that, indeed, in fact, actually happened? Not whether you did it, but whether in fact that happened from time to time?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the occasion of any enquiry or the gathering of information or reporting somewhere, in the category entitled "general information," it would be indicated whether the person in question was a member of the armed forces, or a member of the police force, or a civilian. So we would indicate that. Therefore, the public prosecutor who was appointed and he was at Srebrenica and he would decide and assess the case and he would decide whether it was necessary to refer it to the military Tribunal at Tuzla, or not. I don't know if I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You have. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P507. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I don't know what the controversy was but there was something wrong with the English translation and we now have the correct, full, proper English translation to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of document 507? MR. DI FAZIO: Of document 507 to be handed up. Can I ask that this be substituted? I think this is clearly the better version. And I don't think there is anything but cosmetic changes in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection on your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. I was trying to remember what the controversy was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know which witness it would have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's something important I would have a note, but I don't have a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Something corrected is better than something uncorrected, so no objections. MR. DI FAZIO: Apparently it related to Mr. Bogilovic, but -- Tankic, I'm sorry, but I can't vouch for that and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, so this will be the new P507/E, which will replace the previous 507/E. All right. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, the first question that I need to ask you is, if you go back, at the very back of the document, there is -- I think there is a signature there. Is that your signature? And did you create this document?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm going to lead you to certain parts of -- aspects of the document because I'm sure that they're uncontroversial. First of all it is clear the document is dated July, 28 July 1993. You can see that at the top left-hand part of the page. Can you see that? The very first page.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the 28th here. The 28th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Yes. Now, there is a stamp there as well. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's apparently the stamp of the District Military Prosecutor in Tuzla. Do you see that? And it's dated the 22nd of August, 1993. Got it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't need to go through the whole text of the case. The first question is, are you familiar with this case? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The fellow who was charged was a young man called Emir Halilovic and he was a cousin, I believe, of the -- of Mr. Halilovic who was in charge of military police.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirza's, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And he -- tell me if this is correct: Did you investigate the case or your offices investigate the case?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm always afraid that I might take up too much time. Yes, we did try to investigate, to no avail, and I myself got involved directly and I investigated this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. That's just fine. That's exactly what I wanted to know. Now, this fellow, Emir, did he become upset at the death of Mirzet Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Anyway, he killed these people, Slobodan Zekic [phoen] and his mother, by hitting them with a pistol, correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: These people were Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay. But that was Serbs? The victims?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In your investigation of the case, was there anything to indicate that they were killed for any other reason other than the fact that they were Serbs? He got upset at what had happened to his cousin and killed these people?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may try and assist you here. Look, when these two people, the mother and the son, were killed, it was in 1992 when the chief of police was Becir Bogilovic. His cousin, Mirza, had not died yet and he carried out this killing and then another one. And then we discovered that he was guilty of the other one. And so it was about both of them. So first of all, we discovered in the course of our investigation we discovered these things. He killed Stojan Krsmanovic on the 27th of July, 1993, when I became chief. And the reason why I indicated this first was that I wanted to have a proper sequence of events. It had happened first. And then I indicated the other thing. If you read through the text, if, you read through this report, you will see that he carried out two different points in time he committed two murders. And the first one was prior to my time as chief and the second one, in the course of my term of office. And then in the course of our investigation we discovered that he was guilty of the same crime in 1992 so we included it in the same criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine, fine?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there anything else that is not clear? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, no, that's good. Thanks very much. Thanks for helping out. But all I want to get to is the motive of the crime. As far as you were able to ascertain. First of all, it says, in your -- Your Honours will find this at page 2. During the fighting for the defence of Srebrenica, Mirzet Halilovic, also known as Mirza, and Emir Halilovic's cousin was killed on the 16th of January 1993. You go back to the first page, and it seems that on almost a month later, on the 10th of February, 1993, while the fellow was drunk, he went to this house and there he killed the lady, the old lady and her son, who were Serbs. Now, all I want to know is, from your investigation, what you know about the case, did this fellow, Halilovic, get upset at the death of his cousin, get drunk and go around and kill these people because he they were Serbs. Not because of any particular dealings or relationships that he had with the two, the two Serbs? Is that your understanding, if it's not tell me?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I didn't know exactly what year it was in. All I said was that at the time there was Halilovic be cheer who was the chief of the police. It was the 10th of February. Now you've reminded me that, about Mirza. Mirza had been killed before. He might have been upset by that. I'm not a psychologist. I mean, I couldn't ask for a doctor's opinion at the time as to what his motives could have been. But he did that. We had irrefutable proof of him having done that and he perpetrated that crime against citizens of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you I won't pursue the matter any more. But one thing is clear: You were able to investigate that matter, prepare this criminal report and send the report off to the district military Prosecutor in Tuzla. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation wasn't good. And this was an action which came out, and there were pretets [phoen] from the citizens of Bosniak nationality and they were -- we were all upset about it. And Naser and I discussed it and we wrote a letter to the son of the victim together and through the Red Cross we delivered the body and we said that we were very sorry about it, because it was the father of a colleague of ours. I mean, that person was drunk and he was lost in the woods and then he entered Srebrenica. If we are talking about the second part. And as to the first part, I mean through UNPROFOR we had to ask for a helicopter because we had no other way. We had to ask for UNPROFOR to take him from our premises because according to our legal provisions I had the right to detain him for up to three days. And anything longer was not possible at that time. So I had to have him removed somewhere else and for the same reason, in agreement with the UNPROFOR commander, we had the Canadian soldiers there, so we agreed that they would take him to Tuzla by helicopter, along with the criminal report and the documents that we managed to put together. We had a camera and we filmed it because we could not have any other photo documents. We had to adjust to the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough. Yes, next question, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did you discuss it with Naser? "Mr. Oric," I should say. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed it when we discovered who he was and I remember, we were together with the Red Cross, International Red Cross people. It is -- remained etched in my memory. We were in front of the Dom Kulture. I myself was writing the letter but we drafted it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So he helped you out. He helped you get to the bottom of this case? Facilitate the process of bringing this man --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one. No. It was about the body being returned. Nobody was an obstacle to that. We did have problems afterwards with certain individuals from the area of Potocari who came and surrounded the police station and asked UNPROFOR for help. And they sent some people who surrounded the police station and we tried to make sure that these people don't get him out of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But as far as Mr. Oric was concerned, he helped you in whatever way he could, to bring the --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- bring this matter to a conclusion and get a -- bring the matter to justice?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic thank you very much for answering my questions. If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I do, however, before I finally sit down, I do have copies of -- four copies now of the -- we have one extra page which bears the name of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was exhibit number, P? MR. DI FAZIO: That was --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 296. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, 296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are going to start with your cross-examination and that will be conducted, in the charge of Madam Vidovic. The only difference that there is going to be is that while Mr. Di Fazio was speaking in English and his questions were being translated to you into Serbo-Croat, Madam Vidovic will be speaking in your own language and therefore you will not be receiving interpretation. There will be no need for interpretation. From our experience here, that causes problems, because you will not allow a sufficient time before you answer her question to make it possible for the interpreters to translate to us in English what you -- what is being said in B/C/S. So I am going to make an appeal to both of you, to you, Mr. Meholjic, and Madam Vidovic, to allow a short interval of time between question and answer and between answer and question so that the interpreters that are behind you have got sufficient time to translate what is being said into English and into French. All right? And I count on your cooperation. Otherwise, we will have -- we will encounter problems. Madam Vidovic is already aware of this because you're not the first one to come here and give evidence in Serbo-Croat. Yes, Madam Vidovic he is all yours Cross-examined by Madam Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Meholjic. I have prepared quite a few questions for you and I would like to kindly ask you that whenever possible and to the extent possible, you try to answer my question with a simple yes or no, especially the first part of my questions that have nothing to do with documents. In order to save time, obviously, that in case you're in agreement with what I'm asking you. Mr. Meholjic, you, in the course of your testimony, have mentioned that you were a police officer, had been a police officer a long time before the war, including the prewar period?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You are familiar with the circumstances and events connected to the preparations for war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what I'm particularly interested in is the area of Podravanje.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a considerable extent this is well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Preparations for the war at Podravanje were clearly visible already in the course of 1989 in your area, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I can't be sure what you are hinting at, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm going to clarify. You are aware, as a prewar police officer, that the SDB from Serbia in August 1989 started a campaign aimed at proving the purported fact that the Serbs were under threat in a part of Bosnia and in the municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac in particular, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There were rumours that were launched, amongst them the alleged report of the SDB of Serbia from August 1989 stating that Serbs were leaving the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac under the pressure of Muslim fundamentalists. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This report was checked. It was verified and the police station in which you worked participated in that verification as well?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Several commissions were set up, one of them at the state level and it was established that this report was false, that it was not true. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the goal of all of these rumours was to win over all of the Serbs to one side?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The local media from the Birac region were connected with the Serbian media and together they launched these rumours. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: During the year 1991, along the borders of the Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina and Serbia, on the Serbian side, the weapons and artillery pieces of different calibres were located, and their barrels were directed towards Srebrenica. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The activists of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, were closely cooperating with the JNA in this area. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only closely, but fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Mr. Meholjic. They supplied weapons from Serbia and located these weapons in Serbian villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: They also distributed these weapons amongst the Serbian population of mixed villages?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did bring weapons to three areas by the helicopters of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about certain names within the context of the Serbs in the area being armed. And before that, let me just ask you to clarify something. You said that weapons were brought by helicopters into three regions. Can you please state the names of these regions?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zalazje, Brezani, and Podravanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, perhaps it's the case of asking the witness to confirm whether -- how he came -- how he came by this, to know about this, whether he knows it first hand or whether he knows it second-hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, you've heard the Presiding Judge. And let me put the following question to you. You were a policeman in 1991. Am I right in saying that such developments were within the scope of your authorities, that you were privy to such information?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We even carried out the analysis of political and security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So I would be right in saying that in the course of your -- the performance of your duty, you came by this information?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When it comes to arming the Serbian population, does the name Slavko Jovanovic, does this name ring any bells, the person from Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is it true that you heard his name within the context of Serbs being armed?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Does the name of Milan Suncin ring a bell within this same context?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of Rasa Milosevic from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he amongst the persons who organised the arming of Serbs in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It is true, Mr. Meholjic, that the Serbs in Podravanje were armed before the war started?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Srebrenica and Bratunac, there were camps where Serbian soldiers were trained long before the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a lot about that. We verified that information. We obtained some information, but I was never on the spot. I was never in any of these places. But, it is a well known fact that they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: One of these camps was in the area of Ratkovici, or to be more precise in Vranesevic, the place is call Ruljevic, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Muslims from Poznanovici, much before the war complained about being harassed and disturbed by the shooting coming from this area, the area of Ratkovici and Vranesevici are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From the month of March 1992, the Serbian artillery was deployed on all the strategic points around Srebrenica. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Many units of the JNA which had been withdrawn from the Republic of Croatia ended up in the area of Podrinje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am so sorry to interrupt you. It shouldn't happen. It's the second time that I hear you say Podrinje, and in the transcript I read "Podravanje." And this is, if you look at line 13 on the previous page, again it is repeated. So this is a matter that needs to be attended to later. Okay. It's a mistake. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No, Your Honour, and I thank you very much for drawing my attention to it. I am talking Podrinje, which is a much broader area than the village of Podravanje. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I said that many units of the JNA that had been withdrawn from Croatia ended up in Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The armoured brigade of the JNA from Jastrebarsko, after having withdrawn from the Republic of Croatia, moved all of its equipment from, to Podrinje and its command post was in Paprace. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from, but I know that they ended up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you were aware of the fact that this brigade had its command post in Paprace, in central Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of its commander, Radoslav Tatic [phoen], a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear his name come up in conversations but I never got to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the problem that can be resolved, whether the witness -- please, witness, can you explain to the witness what Podrinje is, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the area through which the river Drina flows and all of the places in that valley, the common name of that area is Podrinje and it encompasses all of these municipalities such as Srebrenica, Bratunac, and other municipalities. It is a general term for the Drina valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have another witness who --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This was just for the record and thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The Serbian forces occupied the municipality of Zvornik, thus cutting Srebrenica off from Tuzla. And this happened on the 8th of April, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The line around Srebrenica continued when the armoured brigade from Jastravaco [phoen] was deployed in the village of Lukic Polje near Milici; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The villagers of Milici had their own military formation, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in Milici. All of the villagers had their respective military formations. Not just the villagers of Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you that. All of the Serbian villages around Srebrenica and Bratunac as early as March 1992 had their own military formations of the Territorial Defence, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And if I may add to that, at a meeting of the police in Srebrenica when we discussed that, a certain number of Serbs, whose name -- a certain a certain Serb whose name I can mention but maybe the person doesn't want his name to be mentioned. He told us, and he cried when he said that all the territorial -- Serbian defence units came under the control of the JNA. His name was Milun Prendic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. During the early days of April 1992 Srebrenica was cut off from Han Pijesak, and so was Zepa. Han Pijesak was to become the command centre of the Serbian army, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At that time the Serbs blew-up the facility called Kvarc which was the -- one of the relays of the Bosnian television and by doing that they placed the citizens of Srebrenica in media isolation?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. And let me add to that, that the repeaters of the public security station of Srebrenica also existed on that relay and when this was blown up, we were cut off from the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There was no cooperation of Serbian policemen investigating such events. In other words, they basically blocked such investigations?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some did. Some did not. Some were in favour of the war. We held meetings with them. We spoke to some others who were honest and came under threat because they did not obey, as they didn't want this war. They cried at our meetings, which were common meetings of Muslims and Serbs. None of us wanted the war. But, some of our policemen worked for their counter-intelligence. There were others who were honest and loyal.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just clarify something with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that some of them did not obey the SDS. This was something that has been omitted from the record.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that some of them did not obey the SDS. And they told us that at a meeting. The meeting of all of us who worked in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the Serbian policemen who did not obey the SDS came under threats, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The police station of Srebrenica, under those conditions in April, could no longer work as a single unit and it was transformed into seven smaller police stations: Srebrenica, Osac [phoen], Skelani, Suceska, Sase, Brezani, and Potocari. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their numbers, but you are right. My superior officer would know that, and it was the chief of police who decided on that. I was not in the position to know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As early as the 13th of April, 1992, there were first casualties amongst the Muslims, Mehoric [phoen] From Potocari and Osmanovic Saba Hudin from Gostojevo [phoen] were killed on the way to their respective homes. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed. They went up to Skelani. That's where they were killed. And they were found somewhere near Kraglijivoda or Vitez. I can't tell you anything more precise had I than that. There is a place called Vitez near Kraglijivoda. I believe that that is where their bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their dead bodies were found there. The police went up there to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've told us that on the 17th of April, 1992, the Serbian Democratic Party, headed by Deronjic and Zekic asked people from Srebrenica to lay down their weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and this was done together with the JNA. But this happened in Bratunac. The people from Bratunac were asked to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about the people from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was too fast. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I will clarify that with you. Witness, please, people from Srebrenica were asked to come to Bratunac and in Bratunica [as interpreted], the Muslims of Srebrenica were given this ultimatum to surrender their weapons. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The president of the SDS of Bratunac, Miroslav Deronjic, gave an ultimatum to the Muslim leadership and he told them: "Muslims in Srebrenica have to surrender their weapons. It has been decided that this part of Bosnia will become a Serbian Bosnia." You know that because the participants in the meeting told you that immediately after the end of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that you were not going to surrender your weapons. You took to the woods and you invited anybody who wanted to join you to come with you and that's how you took to the woods. It is correct that Srebrenica came under attack on the following day, on the 18th of April, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The Serbian forces entered Srebrenica. From then up to the 9th of May 1992 many citizens of Srebrenica were either killed or went missing. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And some of them were burned alive in their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Many of those people who had not been killed were captured, and they ended up in camps in the surrounding Serb villages and they were subjected to torture there. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were killed and some of them were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You also told us that many houses in Srebrenica were torched at that time, including your own. It was more than 80 houses at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but you can find out and at any rate, quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There was looting of everything that could have been taken away? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No gold was left at Srebrenica after the Serb units. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was left behind the of. The people were asked to give everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If anyone were to claim that gold from Srebrenica was looted by Naser Oric, it would not be correct, would it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not be correct, but can we clarify something? At Srebrenica we had a production plant, the 11th of March, and they processed the Silver from Srebrenica. And I -- my -- and one person with his men came afterwards. And then the other person sold it to me at Tuzla afterwards. I mean, Naser has nothing to do with it. Desnica Radivojevic had something to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for clarifying that. Systematic and destructive attacks followed against other Muslim villages around Srebrenica in the direction of Bratunac? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started. I don't know where all of these offences took place. I was trying to save my life. But all sorts of things were happening and at a later stage I found out about what was going on where, but at that particular moment I only followed the events in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out about horrible atrocities taking place at the primary school Vuk Karadzic in Bratunac and in the area of Bratunac against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My grandmother was killed. She was 103 years old and she is my mother's mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. Meholjic. - Madam Vidovic please try to allow a small interval of time, a short interval of time between question and answer, because you're jumping straight one on to the other straight away. Sometimes not even allowing the question to finish or the answer to finish. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you hear about the inhabitants of Glogova, Hranca, Voljevica, Kauz [phoen] disappearing?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about shooting as well at Glogova, around the mosque. I heard about Voljevica because my mother was from Voljevica. I also heard about what was going on at Bratunac because my next door neighbours, Mirsa Begic, could not even get out of Srebrenica and they did not have a gun or anything and were not allowed to. And then they were stopped, took to school and then they were killed and tortured, et cetera. And their eyes were being taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Meholjic. Are you aware of the fact that Muslims from Sikiric, Bjelovac, Abdulic, the area of Zanjevo were chased away in the course of the first two months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know about that. This is a Bratunac area. Srebrenica, Skelani, up there. Everything. Wherever there was mixed population or the villages were close. I mean the Serb and the Muslim villages, the Muslims had to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You mentioned Skelani. Isn't it correct that the Skelani area, before the war, had an overwhelming majority of Muslim population; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Likari was attacked from the direction of Bjelovac and Sase by the end of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I heard from other people, yes. I was not at Likari at that time but I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Madam Vidovic. We will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, you're aware of the fact that by the beginning of the war, the Muslims who fled to Serbia, Montenegro were sent back, captured and killed, so according to orders from Miroslav Radic [phoen] from Bratunac, a whole group of people on a bus coming back from Serbia and Montenegro, including your brother, Malik Meholjic, were killed, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So columns of refugees -- or rather this situation has caused columns of refugees, thousands of them, at least 40.000 of them descended upon Srebrenica in the summer of 1992, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is it not true that those people had nothing to live on, there was no food, no medicines, no water, no electricity?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just for them. There was nothing for us who were at home there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meholjic. Is it not correct that only several hundred pre-war inhabitants remained in Srebrenica and they, too, found themselves in an extremely difficult situation with regard to food, clothes, medicines, and everything else?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Chaos reigned. People were exposed to daily shelling, snipers during that period?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The situation was similar in other Muslim villages surrounding Srebrenica, Konjevic Polje, Cerska, they too were packed with refugees, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask the clerk to show a document to the witness. It is a document issued by the War Presidency of Srebrenica, number 7/92 of the 21st of September 1992. Addressed to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Chief of Staff of the armed forces and the public in general. Mr. Meholjic, I'm going to quote to you a shorter part of that document and I will ask you about your opinion. It says: "The situation in the area of Srebrenica is still extremely difficult. From the Chetnik stronghold Drogic [phoen] multi-barreled rocket launchers shelled Potocari and Suceska. Fortunately, no one was killed or wounded, but there was a great deal of material damage. In the area of Oset [phoen] and Kraglijivoda there were tank attacks and Howitzer attacks from the hydro electric power plant. Peratic [phoen] area, the hills of Tara [phoen] in Serbia and the stronghold Jezero in the occupied territories. A convoy of humanitarian aid, which three days ago reached Srebrenica, has not to this day reached its destination or rather" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speaker corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "set out three days ago and has not arrived to its destination to this day. According to the news on the radio of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the convoy was turned back at Bratunac ten kilometres short of the final destination. So from the door basically, from the door in, supposedly because of mine fields, about 40.000 people living in this martyred area are asking the representatives of UNPROFOR whether mine fields could have been demined and whether it was absolutely necessary for this convoy to be turned back."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I'm going to ask you in connection with this, in connection with this document, I mean, whether this document does, indeed, reflect the situation in Srebrenica, non-stop shelling from the positions in the surrounding Serb villages and the strongholds in Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it is rather understated, if we think in terms of what the situation really was. Because we had air attacks from Ponikve and of course you could not demine. I mean, the convoy was turned back at Ljubolje [phoen], at the bridge. We saw it on TV afterwards and some women and I know who they were. They stopped the convoy and they wouldn't let them through. So there were no mine fields. They could have travelled through. The representatives of the international community travelled that road on a regular basis. There was no demining to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just said that Srebrenica was shelled by planes. Is it not correct that in the period from the beginning of the war until demilitarisation, there were 37 such attacks?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I myself, tried to shoot those planes and Naser said "Well, why are you chasing them away from here then they go to Potocari and they attack us."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So it is indeed true that the convoys of humanitarian aid were stopped because Serbs simply did not allow for them to go through?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I would like for this document of the War Presidency to be attributed a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D242, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document which is being tendered by the Defence is being admitted and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document which is being tendered by the Defence is being admitted and marked as document D242. Incidentally, Mr. Di Fazio, I'm addressing you, understanding -- fully realising that perhaps you can also tell me, I will have to consult the leader of -- lead counsel on the team. Is the Prosecution in this case contesting that there were -- that Srebrenica, at the relevant time and before, were under constant attack? Or that there were these 35 or 36 or 37 aerial attacks or? Because if it's not, it can save us a lot of time and a lot of questions. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to -- I'm just asking a question. I'm not expecting an answer now. So if you want to consult with Mr. Wubben too, so that you can be give -- anyway it's up to you. MR. DI FAZIO: No, I don't need to consult. There has never been any contest, from the Prosecution's point of view, of the fact that Srebrenica was surrounded by a hostile, aggressive enemy and that conditions there were appalling. In fact, we've led evidence of that. We don't shrink from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that basically means -- yes, Madam Vidovic let me hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just reply. As a matter of fact, it is about the Prosecution trying to prove all the time that Serb villages had some kind of neighbourhood watch systems and we are trying to show that the military action was justified and that's why I'm asking witnesses about these facts. In the same way we've asked for the acceptance of the Deronjic ruling and it was basically with regard to the fact that the Deronjic ruling facts could be taken as established and the Prosecution was against it, so it is important for me to point out the military situation, characterising the area and the villages around Srebrenica. The Prosecution is not actually against it, but he is trying to prove something totally different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, it is true, isn't it, that the Muslim villages in that area, after the beginning of war, and up to the end of that year, were separated from each other? They were not connected?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were connected. Some of them were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me go one step after another. In Mocovici [phoen] and in Poznanovici, there were refugees, is that correct? A lot of refugees?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mocovici and Poznanovici, in the spring and early summer of 1992 were cut off from Srebrenica and isolated?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were cut off by the village of Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It is also true that at that time Pribicevac was a very strong Serbian military stronghold?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it was reinforced by the JNA. A JNA officer, captain today, a Captain Todorovic [phoen], a very handsome man was there. He was killed there. And his documents were found on the spot. He hailed from Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: These villages were under constant attack from the surrounding Serbian villages, I'm referring to the beginning of war, the summer and spring ever 1992. Are you aware of what?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw with my own eyes. I saw that person. I know personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The villagers of Norici [phoen], Besici, Stedra, Stedric, Pomol, Djile, Johovaca [phoen], Gornja and Donja Virsenje [phoen] which were all Muslim villages and they belonged to the municipality of Vlasenica during the spring and early summer of 1992 these villagers were expelled and arrived in the area of Suceska. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I only heard stories. I didn't see it myself, because it is closer to Suceska, which is in the opposite direction and they could see it better than I could. I know that they were in that area of Konjevic Polje for example is in the area of Suceska and Kusan [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know that they under constant of the Serbian units from the area of Milici, including Rupovo Brdo, Podrinje and Hranca which were the Serbian positions there?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thousands sands upon thousands of people from Glogova, Hranca, Suha, Borkovac, were trying to return to their villages to try and live there throughout the entire year of 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Many of these people, during the year 1992, were killed in ambushes as they were trying to return to their villages and get some food, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a lot of people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: They were also falling victim to mine fields, which could be found everywhere on all the roads that could lead them to their villages, including Korita, Potok, Polje; am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I believe that we even had a record stating that about 4900 people were killed in that area before the beginning of 1993. There are people who know exactly how many people were killed. There was even official information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So they were killed in ambushes and in minefields?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: People who were expelled from Bjelovac, Sase, Voljevica, Abdulic, were also trying to return throughout the war part of the year 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also a lot of them were killed in that attempt. They did the spring sowing. During the war the Serbs did not take the opportunity to get that food, so many people went during the winter and were killed. It was snowing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that a large number of refugees came to Srebrenica. Srebrenica could not bear the pressure of so many refugees?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't. It is a small place, surrounded by hills. And it was as if you were trying to pour one and a half litres of water into a one-litre container. It is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that the situation deteriorated by the day during the late spring and summer of 1992 due to the constant shelling from the reinforced Serbian positions around Srebrenica, am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Srebrenica was constantly shelled from the direction of Nemici [phoen], we were shelled from the Republic of Serbia, from Sateri [phoen], from elsewhere. They were shelling us from all over the place with multiple rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And now let me move on to another topic. Muslim units, the ones that you have spoken about - if I may call them so - to a large extent were cut off from each other. They were not in contact during the spring and summer of 1992. When I say that, I'm referring to the units in the villages that were a bit further from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were no units there. We didn't know who was willing to put up resistance. There were no units. I just took to the woods. I didn't know what would happen next, and I didn't -- we didn't know whether there would be anybody else taking up rifles and joining the defence. At the beginning there were no units. There were just small units. One of them -- or groups. One of them with Naser. One of them with me. These were not formations. They were not legal or semi-legal. They were just tiny groups of people gathered around individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that every of these groups of people were geared towards the defence of their own villages. They were very much local oriented weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were defending the area where they found themselves. They were local units. Or local groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've told us also that the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica was established and that Naser Oric was appointed its commander. The Prosecutor has shown you his document, P73, a decision allegedly issued by the Srebrenica TO in Bajramovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask the usher to present this document to the witness again. The document is P73.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you please look at this decision once again. This is a decision issued on the 20th of May, 1992, allegedly in Bajramovici. You confirmed that these people became members of the body which was set up in Bajramovici. These people are from certain villages, Potocari, Suceska, Bajramovici, Bojna, Ljiesa [phoen] and Srebrenica itself. You can see it in the document can't you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me put a few questions to you in this regard. You will agree with me, won't you, that there were many other villages in the territory of Srebrenica and Bratunac which had armed groups of people, but these villages did not subscribe to the agreement in Bajramovici. Will you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "subscribe." If somebody invited them, they were supposed to give a reason why they were not present. But I will agree that there were some armed groups of people which were not represented by -- at this meeting, and were not encompassed by what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You will agree with me and you have also told us, but let's clarify, that the Muslim villages, some of the Muslim villages were isolated and there were -- there were Serbian forces among those villages.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You will also agree, then, that under such circumstances their communication was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I put it to you that many villagers in the Srebrenica and Bratunac area did not know anything about the agreement that was achieved in Bajramovici. Will you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You knew Fadila Turkovic [phoen] who was a policeman before the war and a commander of the police station in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first knew him as a driver and when the SDA came into power, they appointed him commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But you did know him?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that he rallied around himself a large group of refugees from Vlasenica who arms and who had arrived in the general area of Suceska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This unit was never under the command of Zulfo Tursunovic, was it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because he had to flee. Because he betrayed Vlasenica and he had to flee to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that this unit participated in the fighting around Rupovo Brdo and Podravanje during 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I am not aware of who attacked Rupovo Brdo, that was very far from me. And I did not have any contacts with anybody. Nobody informed me about that. It is possible that you are right. I'm not ruling out anything. I know that Fadil was killed there in the area of Zepa, and as for his group, who was in charge of this group, who was its leader, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you have anything similar information about Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that people from Zepa participated but they may have participated as well. People from Zepa -- everybody now says if you ask them where they hale from they will say they were from Srebrenica. I was in Tuzla when a guy came to beg at my door. I asked him where he was from, he said he was from Srebrenica. I said where from. He said, "I'm not from Srebrenica, I'm from Zvornik." So when we're talking about this event everybody says he was from Zepa. Whether he was from Zepa or not, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Have I understood you correctly that units from Zepa, possibly Turkovic's units participated in the battles around Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I did say in my statement that there were some Zepa people, but they could have come in from some of the surrounding villages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Those units, so there were many other armed groups which for a longer period of time, perhaps all the way up to demilitarisation acted independently. Are you aware of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know how other people acted. For the simple reason -- I mean I really want to tell the truth here, and nothing more but the truth. Probably there was something like that, but I really don't know what the line of command was for Logova [phoen] et cetera. I don't know that. I know what I know. I know what I've told you here. And I know about my participation. And I know I take full responsibility for moral, material, and criminal responsibility for everything I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meholjic, these units that we talked about, generally speaking, offered resistance in the course of the summer -- no, spring, summer, and autumn 1992, at least until the 14th of October. They offered resistance, but they had a -- local commanders and they had a local organisation as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you clarify your question, because it is not clear to me. Some of them did act and others didn't. I was one of those who acted as I felt was right, and that's what I did. I have nothing to hide. As to what other people did, I don't know. There was staff there, as it was. They know who acted within it, who acted outside. I'm not somebody who has full knowledge of all of these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, if you look at the previous question, and then your last question, this is the problem. Because to your previous question, the witness had not agreed with what you were suggesting. And you simply ignored the answer that he gave you and assumed that he had agreed or put another question assuming that he was agreeing with the position as submitted to him by you, which is not the case. So he has never -- he told you straight "I don't know how other people acted." He told you he didn't know, he can't give you information about these other units. And then you ask him precisely what these other units were supposed to have been doing. So let's move, if you have a more concrete way of approaching this particular matter, you please go ahead. If not, please go ahead with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the essence of my question to the witness was whether it was self-organised structure. Nobody set up those groups, but they got organised themselves in the beginning of the war. And for a certain period during the war. Whether they got organised themselves, that was the essential of my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the case with me, and that was a group that got together on their own initiative and then, afterwards, everything else I've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you Mr. Meholjic. As to the decision about the setting up of the so-called, the Territorial Defence for Srebrenica Staff or that body that was formed on the 20th of May, 1992, you will agree that at Bajramovici the decision was made by an informal group of people, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to my assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the legal provisions that applied then of the former Yugoslavia, that such a decision would have had to be made by a social-political body, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Since the decision was made by an informal group of people, it was not adhered to by all the armed groups and individuals, wasn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that that is probably one of the reasons why you, inside Srebrenica, did not consider that decision to be binding for you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that we had to do something, coordinate something. But I was of the opinion that it had to be done in a different way. And I thought that it was illegal, from my point of view. I think I've mentioned it. I still don't know whether it was legal or not. But my assessment at the time was that it was not legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In other words, you did not consider that agreement at Bajramovici as an -- as a State act and therefore you did not act in line with it.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you mentioned that at Bajramovici Naser Oric was appointed commander. You were of the opinion that it wasn't a good solution, wasn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In reply to the Prosecution's question as to whether Mr. Tursonovic tried to convince you to accept Oric as commander, you replied that -- actually, you said that he had told you in case it doesn't go well, things could change. It is not a matter that I myself personally refused, accepting Oric, it was a matter of the overall situation. It was very difficult to do anything that was appropriate, considering the situation and I was of the view that he was not capable of living up to the task. And in connection with this I'm going to ask you a following question. You believed that Oric was not up to the task because he was a young man. He was only 25 years old, and had no military experience, except doing his military service in the former JNA, and more specifically he had no command experience. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Plus the situation was rather complex. And one needs some life experience as well, and I was of the view that -- well, he as a person was a different matter. But with regard to that job, I felt it was too much of a burden for all of us and let alone one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Zulfo Tursunovic told you at the time things might change. Naser might be replaced later, if things don't go well. Do you agree that Naser Oric did not impose himself and did not ask to be appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you agree that Naser was elected or selected as the commander because he was a young, charismatic and popular person?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather tend to say people who were discussing the whole issue, they were counting on the fact that he was a member of the special forces with Milosevic and he had some training, because they were given special training and that's why they felt he could do something. And I think that was the reason, even though I was of the view that the commander did not necessarily have to be a good fighter. But I felt that he had to be able to draw on some life experience and have a different view of life, because he was young, lively and -- well, that was my opinion. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I don't have any objection to the direction of this cross-examination and the matters that Madam Vidovic is raising. I have no problem at all with that. However, you should be made aware of the basis on which these answers are coming. For example, Madam Vidovic asked the witness "Do you agree that Naser was elected or selected as commander because he was young, and charismatic and a popular person." Now, if that was something that is based on knowledge of events at Bajramovici, bearing in mind that he wasn't there, then that should be stipulated; or, whether it is something he knows about because he later found out about, that should be stipulated as well. Otherwise you end up with answers that you won't be able to evaluate later on, and I suggest that the basis for his opinions and anything he may say about events at Bajramovici should be made really clear to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you are 100 per cent right, Mr. Di Fazio. And I think the witness has heard what you said and he will make a statement accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. But if I may respond to that very briefly. My learned friend from the Prosecution put a number of questions yesterday about the meeting in Bajramovici, including who was present, the citizens, the army. All the although the witness wasn't at that meeting and that is why I've been putting wasn't at that meeting and that is why I've been putting questions about Bajramovici, in any case I am going to abide by your suggestion, Your Honours, and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is very little time left to move on, Madam Vidovic. Perhaps the witness -- did you understand what Mr. Di Fazio said? In other words you have been making statements on, such as that from your knowledge Mr. Oric never asked to be appointed commander and, secondly, that you've given your own interpretation or belief of why he was chosen. How do you come to these conclusions? Because you were not there in Bajramovici? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zulfo told me all that when I met with him in the Domavija hotel. He wanted to persuade me to accept Naser as commander. I told him at that moment that I did not perceive Oric as a person fit for a commander, due to his age, lack of experience. I believe that that is what I said and you can find it on the record. I've already said that. Zulfo conveyed to me what was discussed up there, just in rough outlines. This person is no longer amongst us. You cannot confirm this with him. Zulfo asked whether this person had to have a university degree or not. This is what Zulfo told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meholjic. I will end today's day with my next question. Mr. Meholjic Mr. Oric was not appointed because of his maturity, experience, military knowledge education, or any similar thing, is that correct? As far as you know?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know he wasn't. He was appointed for the things that I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will have to leave it at that for today. We will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Let's go into private session for one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
